guide.title: Secondary Assessment
guide.lead: After the life threats are handled, look properly. Go head to toe for big mechanisms and unresponsive patients, or do a focused exam for one clear complaint. In a time-critical patient, do it en route, never at the cost of transport.

sections.title: Signs worth knowing
rows: Raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, clear fluid from nose or ears
Unequal or unreactive pupils (record size in mm)
Paradoxical movement; crepitus; crackling under the skin
Flail chest; rib fracture; air leak
Seat-belt bruise, bruising around the navel or flanks, rigidity

sections.title: Special handling
items: Pelvis: don't rock it; pelvic binder at the greater trochanters for suspected fracture with shock
Open chest wound: vented chest seal (or an occlusive dressing taped on three sides); watch for tension
Check circulation, motor and sensation (CMS) before and after every splint

quiz.q: A grating sensation over the forearm is:
High-speed crash, alert with chest pain from the steering wheel, stable vitals. Approach?
options: Rapid head-to-toe with attention to the chest: the mechanism warrants it

quiz.explanation: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, Swelling.

options: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light

quiz.q: A section of chest moving in on inspiration:
quiz.explanation: Several ribs broken in more than one place.

quiz.q: A stab wound to the back of the chest, no bubbling. Best dressing?
options: Vented chest seal (or occlusive dressing taped on three sides)
Pelvic binder at the greater trochanters; don't rock the pelvis
Rock the pelvis repeatedly to confirm

quiz.q: When should you skip the detailed secondary exam on scene?
options: Time-critical patients: do it en route

quiz.explanation: CMS in every limb you splint.

flashcards.question: DCAP-BTLS
flashcards.answer: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures/Penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, Swelling.

flashcards.question: Rapid head-to-toe vs focused exam
flashcards.answer: Rapid head-to-toe: significant mechanism or unresponsive. Focused: a stable patient with one clear complaint.

flashcards.question: PERRL
flashcards.answer: Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light. Record size in mm and reactivity.

flashcards.question: Crepitus in a limb
flashcards.answer: Bone ends grating: a fracture. Splint before moving.

flashcards.question: Basal skull fracture signs
flashcards.answer: Raccoon eyes, Battle's sign (behind the ear), clear fluid from the nose or ears.

flashcards.question: CMS
flashcards.answer: Circulation (distal pulse, colour), Motor, Sensation: checked before and after splinting.

flashcards.question: When to skip the full secondary assessment
flashcards.answer: Time-critical patients (arrest, ongoing resuscitation, shock needing surgery): do it en route if at all.

flashcards.question: JVD
flashcards.answer: Distended neck veins: tension pneumothorax, tamponade or heart failure.

critical.scenario: Thrown from an ATV: bleeding scalp cut, deformed left forearm and femur, chest abrasions, left upper quadrant tenderness. Alert, SpO₂ 97%, strong radial pulses. 18 minutes to the trauma centre.
critical.question: Best approach?

options.t: Pressure on the scalp, splint the femur and forearm with CMS checks, IV en route, and reassess the abdomen often during rapid transport
Treat the most visible injury and take your time
options.f: The abdomen is the hidden threat.

options.t: Rock the pelvis to check stability
Full splinting of everything on scene before moving
options.f: Splint during packaging; don't delay transport.

critical.explanation: Left upper quadrant tenderness may be a bleeding spleen: watch for shock.

critical.scenario: A 67-year-old with heart failure, breathless for 3 hours: tripoding, BP 158/94, HR 108, RR 26, SpO₂ 89%. Crackles at both bases, ankle edema, raised JVP.
critical.question: Key finding and priority?

options.t: Crackles with raised JVP and edema: acute heart failure – sit up, oxygen to target, CPAP, nitrates per protocol

options.f: Crackles, JVP and edema point to the heart.

critical.explanation: A focused exam that confirms the field impression.

critical.scenario: Log-rolling a stabbed 22-year-old reveals a second 3 cm wound on the right posterior chest. Breath sounds reduced on the right, trachea midline, BP 110/70, SpO₂ 93%.
critical.question: What do you do with the wound?

options.t: Vented chest seal (or occlusive dressing taped on three sides) and watch for tension pneumothorax

options.f: It can suck air into the chest.
Any chest wound can enter the pleura.

critical.explanation: Signs of tension: worsening hypoxia, raised JVP, falling BP, deviated trachea (late).
